summary: Describes how Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) is used over paths that span more than one IP hop, including paths where traffic may travel in only one direction on a link. It adapts the single-hop approach to longer, routed paths. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Checking that a friend next door is awake is easy. This explains how to check on a friend several streets away, even when messages may take different roads there and back.

questions: how does bfd work across multiple hops
what port does multihop bfd use
why can bfd echo not be used over multiple hops
how does bfd work on unidirectional links
subtitle: How to run BFD liveness checks across several routed hops, where the single-hop tricks no longer work.

tldr.problem: Single-hop BFD relies on a TTL of 255 for spoofing protection and on the incoming link to pick the right session. Neither works when the path spans many hops or overlaps with other paths.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC offers address-pair demultiplexing, out-of-band discriminator signaling and a passive-role method for unidirectional links. It also sends BFD to UDP port 4784, forbids Echo and recommends cryptographic authentication.
tldr.outcome: BFD can monitor arbitrary routed paths between systems, such as OSPF Virtual Links, but is not meant for application-to-application use across the Internet.

today: RFC 5883 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: BFD Beyond a Single Hop
sections.content:
The Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol, defined in RFC 5880, detects liveness on arbitrary paths between systems. The one-hop specification, RFC 5881, covers single hops of IPv4 and IPv6. RFC 5883 covers paths that span multiple network hops and follow unpredictable routes. A pair of systems may also have several paths that overlap.

BFD is an Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) mechanism for connectivity checks and connection verification. It suits network-based services such as router-to-router, subscriber-to-gateway, LSP or circuit endpoints, and service appliance failure detection. Operators must provision the BFD transmit rates correctly to avoid congestion and false failure detection.

It is not applicable to application-to-application failure detection across the Internet, because it cannot detect and avoid congestion and so cannot prevent congestion collapse. Such use would need BFD encapsulated in a transport with TCP-friendly behavior.
sections.eli5: BFD is like two friends tapping a signal back and forth to show they are still there. It is meant for neighbors in the same network, not for strangers across the whole Internet.

sections.title: Three Problems with Multihop Paths
sections.content:
First, spoofing. The one-hop specification avoids spoofed packets by requiring a Time to Live (TTL) or Hop Limit of 255 on send and receive. That cannot work across several hops, so BFD authentication is used instead.

Second, demultiplexing. The first packet of a session may carry a Your Discriminator of zero, so the receiver cannot tell which session it belongs to. Once discriminators are exchanged, packets are matched solely by that field. The one-hop spec solves this by requiring sessions to use independent links, so the first packet is matched by its incoming link. With multihop paths, two paths can overlap to any degree, including the first or last hop, so that scheme fails.

Third, the Echo function MUST NOT be used over multiple hops. Intermediate hops would route the packets back to the sender, so connectivity through the whole path could not be verified.
sections.eli5: There are three snags. Anyone could fake a message, it is hard to tell which conversation a first message belongs to, and a message that bounces back early proves nothing about the far end.

sections.title: Demultiplexing Packets
sections.content:
The RFC gives three approaches, to be chosen according to the application.

Totally arbitrary paths. Limit deployment to a single session per source and destination address pair. Several sessions between the same two systems must differ in at least one endpoint address. The first packet, with Your Discriminator zero, is matched by that address pair. This suits general connectivity detection over routed paths and OSPF Virtual Links.

Out-of-band discriminator signaling. The discriminators are exchanged by another mechanism before the session starts, so no packet with Your Discriminator zero is ever sent. This is used by the BFD MPLS specification. It is simple for BFD and lets other components that know the paths direct it, but it needs some BFD-specific knowledge outside BFD.

Unidirectional links. These count as multihop paths because the return path may be arbitrary and may overlap with others. The Unidirectional Sender MUST operate in the Active role and the Unidirectional Receiver MUST operate in the Passive role. The Passive receiver stays silent until the first Control packet arrives, matches it using the physical or logical link it came in on, and learns the sender's discriminator. It then echoes that value back in its own Control packet over any route, and from then on matching uses discriminators alone.
sections.eli5: If two friends want to talk but cannot tell their chats apart, they can use different phone numbers, agree on secret codes ahead of time, or let one speak first so the other learns the code.

sections.title: Encapsulation on Port 4784
sections.content: Multihop BFD Control packets are encapsulated in IPv4 and IPv6 exactly as in the one-hop specification, with one difference: the UDP destination port MUST be 4784. A separate port helps with demultiplexing and internal routing of incoming BFD packets. IANA has assigned port 4784 for BFD Multihop Control.
sections.eli5: Multihop BFD gets its own mailbox number, 4784, so these messages do not get mixed up with the single-hop kind.

sections.title: Authentication and Security
sections.content:
Multihop paths expose BFD to spoofing, and the exposure grows with the number of hops. Implementations SHOULD therefore use cryptographic authentication over multihop paths to help mitigate denial-of-service attacks. The RFC strongly encourages strong forms of authentication.

It raises no security issues beyond those in the referenced BFD documents.
sections.eli5: The farther a message travels, the easier it is for a stranger to fake it, so each message should carry a secret signature.
